extracted.intended_audience: educators, instructional designers, distance-education researchers, and policy-makers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for selecting, designing, and assessing interactive online learning media, including Web 2.0/3.0 technologies, social software, open-source solutions, and access considerations for diverse contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet affordances and limits for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet offers a means for gaining the attention of learners, and of presenting opportunities for focusing perceptions and prompting recall; learner participation can be supported, especially with computer-mediated communications (CMC) and collaborative learning projects. Providing instruction and assuring appropriate organization, sequencing, and higher-order outcomes are less easily accomplished with the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also note practical constraints: much online content is effectively a one-way presentation of information; the reliability of information on the Internet may be suspect; and successful use currently demands proficient literacy and computer skills. Use the Internet for attention, engagement, and participation, but be cautious about relying on it alone for structured instruction and higher-order learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web 2.0 as a pedagogical resource ('writing web')
rubrics_metrics.description: Web 2.0 is characterized by tagging, social networks, and user generation of content, using tools such as Wikis, blogs, and podcasts. Web 2.0 is called the 'writing web' because it allows individual users to create and circulate their own materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage Web 2.0 tools to enable learner-generated content and two-way communication; these tools help redress the one-way nature of earlier web publishing and support collaborative authoring (e.g., wikis) and reflective public writing (blogs, podcasts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Web 3.0 / Semantic Web capabilities and prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth and acceptance of Web 3.0 (the 'Semantic Web') is predicated on: 1) spread of Internet access to millions via mobile devices; 2) growing social interest in the technology; and 3) consistently labelling information so it makes sense to machines as well as people. In Web 3.0, content is encoded so computers can locate and extract the information; software agents will be able to 'troll the Net and find what they're looking for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing for future/semantic-web scenarios, ensure metadata and consistent labeling to support machine readability. Be aware of major challenges: the present Web is described as increasingly 'fragile' and retrofitting metadata to millions of existing items is an immense task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions underpinning next-generation Internets relevant to distance education
rubrics_metrics.description: New-Internet initiatives proceed from several assumptions applicable to virtual and distance education: worldwide Internet growth will continue; world-wide Internet-based research/academic/government/corporate cooperation will continue and increase; the Internet is a powerful tool for productive collaboration and communication; governments have a responsibility to fund and maintain such networks; ease-of-use, power/speed, cost, and accessible content determine wireless growth; designers will strive to make new Internets not more failure-prone as they increase complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these assumptions as design and policy premises when planning educational infrastructures or programs; test locally rather than assuming universal applicability, and consider governance, funding, usability, and resilience when adopting new-network technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality-based access requirements for the developing world
rubrics_metrics.description: In regions lacking reliable infrastructure (e.g., power), sophisticated computer-based communications may be infeasible; technologies must recognize both socioeconomic and technological issues. Alternate-powered technologies (wind-up devices, radios, spring-powered computers, keystroke-powered devices) and mobile/cellular solutions may be more suitable than traditional computer deployments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interventions that fit local infrastructure: prioritize low-power or alternative-power devices, mobile-first solutions, and distribution methods (e.g., satellite downloads to PDAs) that avoid dependency on print. Use evidence (e.g., cellphone coverage and adoption statistics) to guide technology choice for training and learning in low-resource contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core interaction supports provided by social software
rubrics_metrics.description: Social software supports group interaction and, specifically, three types of interaction: (1) support for conversational interaction between individuals or groups (real-time IM to asynchronous collaborative teamwork, including blogs); (2) support for social feedback, where a group rates contributions producing a digital reputation; and (3) support for social networks to explicitly create and manage personal relationships and help develop new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or selecting social software for learning, assess whether and how the tool supports these three interaction types; consider real-time vs asynchronous needs, mechanisms for reputation/feedback, and affordances for relationship-building and network formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical/community affordances of social software
rubrics_metrics.description: Social software can change community function: groups benefit from members acting in more social, community-oriented ways. It emphasizes interpersonal interaction, supporting collaboration, cooperation, social equality, mutual support, voluntary affiliation, intrinsic motivation, democratic governance, and trust. In education, social software encourages collaborative, community-oriented learning where members seek out peers with needed knowledge and contribute to group success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design learning activities to exploit voluntary, interest-driven participation; foster governance and trust mechanisms; emphasize mentoring, personal learning assistance, and shared project work. Be mindful that these affordances rely on community norms and active participation rather than imposed class membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and criticisms of social software for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Social software has critics who argue virtual immersion can be 'a complete waste of time' with 'no hint of reality and its consequences'; virtual worlds have been called 'lawless'. Some evidence suggests social networks lose value as membership increases (exclusivity matters) and participation can be short-lived (e.g., many blogs abandoned within months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and mitigate risks: provide scaffolding to help learners relate online interaction to face-to-face skills, design for sustained participation, manage community size and inclusivity trade-offs, and evaluate whether particular social environments align with learning goals rather than novelty or entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-source advantages for educational technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Open source advocates promote software open to modification and low-cost distribution to support experimentation and competition. A large community of contributors who check each other's work can produce software 'of consistently high relative quality.' Major corporations and institutions support and use open-source projects, and open-source systems (e.g., Linux) have shown rapid adoption in certain domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider open-source options for affordability, flexibility, and community-driven quality assurance. Note institutional and corporate adoption as indicators of maturity for server-side and infrastructure solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-source disadvantages and coordination/IP concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many voices contribute to open-source projects, consensus on 'the right way' can be lacking; this can lead to feature bloat where 'every possible option is built into the software,' frustrating design clarity. There may also be questions about intellectual property rights since no single author is fully responsible for the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh maintenance, governance, feature-scope control, and IP licensing when choosing open-source tools. Plan for clear project governance, criteria for inclusion of features, and explicit licensing to avoid later disputes or unusable complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers to effective online learning and emerging good practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Persistent issues include cost barriers limiting access (especially in developing countries), ongoing need for training of teachers/trainers/learners, administrators and policy-makers misreading or overselling online impacts, overly complex systems and interfaces, and an unclear relation between learning outcomes and technology use (partly under-theorized and partly due to weak research). At the same time, access is improving for some groups and 'some consensus about good practice is emerging.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address barriers through subsidized access where possible, invest in in-service training, set realistic expectations for online transitions, simplify interfaces, and pursue stronger research linking technology to outcomes. Learn from successful models and industry experience rather than assuming technical deployment alone ensures learning gains.
